_expect.name: Lost Orbit Rock - East Face Left (Angry Inch Wall)

ca_lost_orbit_rock_east_face_left_angry_.blurb: This is the left-hand end of the main face of Lost Orbit Rock, a rock formation in the San Bernardino Mountains at roughly 7,400 feet. It has eight routes: five bolted lines and three that take gear. Six of them sit in the 5.10 range, with one 5.6 and one 5.7 at the gentler end, so it suits climbers who are comfortable on moderate-to-hard single-pitch terrain. The face it belongs to is the taller, more sustained side of the formation. Two walk-in trails reach it, one from the south parking area and one from the north, each taking only a few minutes.

ca_fawnskin_tower.blurb: Fawnskin Tower is a small rock tower of about 45 feet on the slope above the town of Fawnskin, in the San Bernardino Mountains near 7,000 feet. All eight routes are trad lines. The grades run from fourth-class scrambling through the 5.5 range up to three climbs in the 5.10 range. The front of the tower is the bigger side and carries most of the climbing, while the back is smaller. The tower stands just above houses rather than out in the backcountry, and finding the way to it can take some patience.

ca_houser_buttress.blurb: Houser Buttress is a tall, narrow, south-facing formation of around 80 feet on the southwest side of the Real Hidden Valley cluster in Joshua Tree National Park, near 4,200 feet. Eight routes are here, seven on trad gear and one top rope. The grades are one 5.9, two in the 5.10 range and five in the 5.11 range, so it works best for climbers already leading 5.10 and up. The face looks smooth from below, and reaching the base involves a short scramble through blocks to a ledge system.
ca_houser_buttress.approach: Follow the marked trail west from the Real Hidden Valley parking lot for a few hundred yards; the last stretch is a short scramble up through blocks to a ledge that leads right to the base.

ca_el_segundo_buttress.blurb: El Segundo Buttress is a high rock buttress above Premier Buttress in the Whitney Portal area near Lone Pine, in the Eastern Sierra, at around 9,000 feet. Eight routes climb it, seven of them trad and one sport. They span 5.9 to 5.11, with one 5.9, three in the 5.10 range and four in the 5.11 range. The longest is a five-pitch 5.9 line, and several others are two-pitch climbs in the 5.11 range, so this is more of a multi-pitch objective than a roadside crag.

ca_devil_boulder.blurb: Devil Boulder is the first boulder you meet from the parking lot at the Catacombs, on the Sherwin Plateau above the Mammoth Lakes area in the Eastern Sierra, at about 7,000 feet. A path drops into a wash to reach it. It has eight problems on pocketed tuff, with a prominent prow as its main feature. Grades run from V0 to V5: three at V0, one V1, one V2, two V3 and a single V5. Some of the rock near the tops is friable, so topping out takes care. Landings in the Catacombs are mostly flat pumice.

ca_false_hueco_boulder.blurb: False Hueco Boulder is an obvious overhanging, northwest-facing block sitting up on a ledge in the Outback, the open valley of boulders north of Hidden Valley Campground in Joshua Tree National Park, at about 4,200 feet. It has eight problems, mostly in the middle of the grade range: one each at V1, V2 and V3, four at V4 and one V5. The Outback is known for tan rock with dark patina patches that make sharp holds, and this boulder is a short walk from the campground loop.

ca_oldsquaw_boulder.blurb: Oldsquaw Boulder, also called Mosquito Rock, stands alone in a flat meadow at Wawona in the southern part of Yosemite National Park, at about 4,250 feet. It is granite, and the level ground around it leaves plenty of room for pads. Eight problems start from a very easy VB up to V3, with most at V1 or V2. A warm-up line gives an easy start, and a couple of harder lines on the central face and a deep corner are for creative boulderers. Few climbers come through, so some lines need a brush before use, and the top can be covered in moss and needles.
